issues.legal_issue: A proposed amendment to a written statement that elaborates the defence and assists in determining the real controversy should be considered liberally where it causes no serious injustice or prejudice.
material_facts: The defendants sought to add facts about the source of the purchase money and the later mutation of the property, describing the changes as an elaboration of their defence.
The proposed amendments raised matters relevant to the dispute over ownership and possession.
The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice from the amendment.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts erred in rejecting the amendment application; the amendment was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court broad discretion to permit amendments needed to determine the real questions in controversy, on just terms. Courts should exercise that power liberally unless serious injustice or irreparable loss would result. Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Hnaung states that amendment powers serve the proper administration of justice but do not permit substitution of one distinct cause of action for another.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and proposed_amendment_elaborates_defence and amendment_assists_real_dispute and no_serious_prejudice

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.proposed_amendment_elaborates_defence: The proposed changes added detail to or developed the defence already advanced.
predicates.amendment_assists_real_dispute: The proposed changes concerned matters relevant to deciding the dispute between the parties.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice or injustice from the proposed changes.

issues.definition: When a written-statement amendment develops the defence, assists resolution of the dispute, and causes no serious prejudice, the amendment should be allowed.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation defence may be added to a written statement by amendment where its applicability is disputed and can be determined as an issue in the suit.
material_facts: The defendants sought to add a defence that the suit was barred by limitation.
Whether limitation barred the suit was disputed and could be determined after the amendment was allowed.
issues.conclusion: The limitation defence could be added by amendment, and its merits could be decided as an issue in the suit.
issues.legal_principle: In Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan, the Court held that an amendment should not be refused merely because the proposed relief may be time-barred where limitation is arguable; the limitation plea can be made an issue after amendment. The dominant purpose of allowing amendment is to minimize litigation.

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.additional_limitation_defence_proposed: The proposed amendment added a defence that the claim was brought too late.
predicates.limitation_applicability_disputed: The parties disputed whether the claim was barred by the applicable time limit.

issues.definition: Where a written-statement amendment adds a limitation defence whose applicability is disputed, that defence may be added and determined in the suit.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement is not barred merely because it is said to withdraw an admission, particularly where no admission is in fact withdrawn and the amendment explains or develops the defence.
material_facts: The original written statement denied that the plaintiff had paid the purchase price and asserted that the parents had sufficient income to purchase the property.
The proposed amendment added that the plaintiff lacked funds and that the property had later been mutated in the names of the plaintiff and defendants in equal shares.
The Court found no admission in the written statement that the proposed amendment sought to withdraw.
issues.conclusion: The amendment could not be rejected on the ground that it withdrew an admission; the proposed changes did not withdraw an admission, and even an admission may be explained by amendment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no admission being withdrawn on the facts. In Estralla Rubber v. Dass Estate (P) Ltd., it was held that even admissions in evidence or in a written statement may be explained by an amendment application.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and (proposed_change_elaborates_existing_defence or proposed_change_explains_admission) and no_serious_prejudice

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.proposed_change_elaborates_existing_defe: The proposed change added detail to or developed a defence already stated.
predicates.proposed_change_explains_admission: The proposed change supplied an explanation for a statement previously made by the defending party.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice or injustice from the proposed change.

issues.definition: A written-statement amendment that develops the defence or explains a prior admission is not barred as a withdrawal of admissions where it causes no serious prejudice.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant may raise inconsistent or alternative defences in a written statement, unlike the restriction applicable to materially altering or substituting a plaintiff’s cause of action.
material_facts: The original written statement asserted that one defendant was the owner and in continuous possession of the property.
The proposed amendment also asserted that, after the parents’ deaths, the property had been mutated in the names of the plaintiff and defendants in equal shares.
The Court held that the proposed defence could not be rejected merely because the pleas were inconsistent.
issues.conclusion: Inconsistent or alternative pleas were permissible in the written statement, and the lower courts erred in rejecting the amendment on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The rules governing amendments to a written statement are not identical to those governing amendments to a plaint: substituting or altering a defence does not present the same problem as substituting a cause of action. M/s. Modi Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. M/s. Ladha Ram & Co. recognizes that inconsistent or alternative pleas may be made in a written statement.

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.alternative_or_inconsistent_defences_pro: The proposed written statement advanced defences that were alternatives to, or inconsistent with, one another.

issues.definition: When a defendant proposes alternative or inconsistent defences in a written statement, those defences are permissible.

issues.legal_issue: Delay alone does not justify rejecting an amendment to a written statement where no serious prejudice or loss of an accrued right is shown.
material_facts: The defendants applied to amend their written statement three years after filing it.
The opposing party was not shown to have suffered serious prejudice that would take away an accrued right.
issues.conclusion: The three-year delay was not, by itself, a sufficient ground to reject the amendment application.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that mere delay in applying to amend a written statement is not a ground for rejection when no serious prejudice is shown to have been caused to the opposing party so as to take away an accrued right.

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.amendment_delayed: The party applied to amend its written statement after a period of time had passed since filing it.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice_to_accrued_right: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice that would deprive it of an accrued right.

issues.definition: Where an amendment application is delayed but causes no serious prejudice to an accrued right, delay alone does not justify rejecting it.

issues.legal_issue: For the restriction on amendments after trial has commenced, trial commences at the final-hearing stage, including examination of witnesses, filing of documents, and addressing arguments.
material_facts: When the amendment application was considered, the parties had yet to file their documentary evidence.
The suit was not at the verge of conclusion, and the final-hearing stages had not taken place.
issues.conclusion: The trial had not commenced, so the restriction on amendments after commencement of trial did not bar the proposed amendment.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure restricts amendments after trial has commenced, subject to the due-diligence exception. The Court construed commencement of trial in this context as the final hearing of the suit, including examination of witnesses, filing of documents, and addressing arguments.

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.documents_not_yet_filed: The parties had not yet filed their documentary evidence in the suit.
predicates.final_hearing_not_started: The suit had not reached the stage of final hearing, including witness examination and addressing arguments.

issues.definition: If a written-statement amendment is sought before documents are filed and before final hearing begins, the trial-stage restriction does not bar the amendment.
